chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya al-Ajaly, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who arranged (the emancipation) of an owned slave of his, a businessman, financially affluent. So the arranged slave buys a slave girl by the order of his master. So she gives birth to children from him. Then the arranged slave dies before his master. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'I view that the entirety of what the arranged slave has left, from wealth or provisions, so it is for the one who had the arrangement for him, and I view that the mother of his children is for the one who had the arrangement, and I view that her children are (all) with the arrangement just like their father. So when the one who arranged for their father were to die, so they are free'.

key_terms.أُمَّ وَلَدِهِ: Mother of his children (concubine who bore his child)
key_terms.دَبَّرَ: Arranged emancipation (partial freedom, full upon master's death)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling for the children and assets of a partially emancipated slave who dies before his master?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the 'dabbir' status is a personal condition attached to the individual rather than a property right, meaning the slave's acquired assets, concubine, and offspring inherit his specific legal standing. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that emancipation is an act of grace by the master, not an automatic transfer of ownership to the slave's estate, ensuring the master retains control until his death. The hadith highlights the intricate interplay between personal status and property rights in classical Islamic inheritance law.
